lesson_title: The Crackle in Your Jersey: Coulomb's Law
hook_text: A balloon you rubbed for three seconds beats the gravity of the entire planet. That is not a trick — that is Coulomb's law.
clip_script: Peel off a jersey on a dry winter evening and it crackles. Rub a balloon on your hair and it parks itself on the ceiling — a balloon, out-pulling the gravitational grip of the ENTIRE Earth. Here is what happened. Rubbing scraped electrons off one surface onto the other. Nothing was created — charge just moved house. And once charges separate, one rule runs everything: opposites attract, likes repel. That is why rubbed hair lifts and spreads — every strand flees its identical neighbours. Want numbers? Same recipe as gravity: multiply the two charges, divide by the distance squared. Positive 3 microcoulombs, negative 5, fifteen centimetres apart: six newtons of pull. And the exam's favourite picture is a tug-of-war: a middle charge with a neighbour on each side. Draw one arrow per neighbour — toward it if they attract, away if they repel. Arrows agree? Add. Arrows fight? Subtract, and the bigger one wins. Arrows first, calculator second. Every time.
visual_style: A dark winter room with static sparks crackling off a jersey; a balloon drifting to the ceiling trailed by tiny charge symbols; then a middle charge stretched in a glowing tug-of-war with two labelled arrows.
mood: Playful and electric — kitchen-table phenomena revealing a clean law.
pacing: Crackling sensory open, calm reveal of the recipe, brisk tug-of-war close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and price any pull or push in newtons.
